In the domain of unsupervised image style transfer, a common evaluation metric is the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), which has a known limitation. This paper proposes an alternative, non-deterministic evaluation framework. Under this framework, we measure the average and variability of output content and perceptual similarity, respectively. Our approach shows that models with lower FID scores do not always represent the best transfer quality. In contrast, our proposed evaluation metrics, ON and PB, provide a more accurate representation of model performance. We demonstrate that models with lower ON and PB scores better match the ground truth performance. Our method also yields better results than USDA in terms of content preservation and style transfer fidelity.

UGC 8839 is an exceptional spiral galaxy that exhibits a dual star formation pattern. It possesses a highly inclined, stable disk maintained by a dark matter halo, and this disk features a long, faint bar along with intense bursts of star creation in its outer segments. On the other hand, the galaxy's central region lacks a prominent bar and exhibits less intense bursts of star creation. What sets UGC 8839 apart is its strongly developing star formation in the far outer reaches of its disk, specifically within the range of 3 to 4 disk scales, a region where most galaxies typically encounter a breakdown in their surface brightness profiles. By utilizing a comprehensive set of optical and near-infrared data along with a sophisticated simulation, we have uncovered the structural, dynamical, and formation history characteristics of the various components within UGC 8839. By breaking it down into distinct regions, we found that its dynamics can be effectively explained by a series of rotating disks moving at right angles to its major axis. Furthermore, we have established that the galaxy's formation has been a highly uneven process, with its outer and inner segments evolving in contrasting ways. On the one hand, its intense outer disk has experienced a relatively balanced and gradual collapse, while its moderate central region has undergone a more violent and irregular formation process that has had a noticeable impact on its Supermassive Black Hole.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, which are massive scale detectors, to find dark matter. These detectors analyze ancient rocks or metals as sensitive detectors, but their effectiveness is limited by impurities in the material. However, some types of rocks such as lunar samples, white sands from the Sahara, and geologic formations from Antarktica have exceptional properties that make them ideal detectors. With their extremely low rates of background noise, these detectors could potentially find certain types of dark matter at a wide range of masses, which includes sub-GeV candidates, at a rate of one event per year or even less.

This paper introduces DP-Sync, a novel framework for secure collaboration between primary users and cloud services in outsourced databases. DP-Sync is based on a secure two-party computation system that incorporates differential privacy to ensure the protection of user actions. The system ensures that user queries are protected against inference by a malicious cloud service, which is possible due to the incorporation of a DP-based update pattern concealment technique. Moreover, DP-Sync allows for efficient user interactions and minimal privacy-related computational overhead. The system also features a robust error-handling mechanism to cope with incorrect queries. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of DP-Sync in achieving robust user-provided queries with minimal impact on system performance.

The extensive use of classification models, including Random Forest (RF), in understanding user behavior and facilitating interactions, relies on identifying crucial features that shape behavior. Despite the capability of RF to assess feature significance, its reliability is compromised by the influence of training data. This study proposes a comprehensive analysis method for machine learning models, with a specific focus on validating significance rankings provided by RF, taking into account user research and adversarial influence. Furthermore, to explore the extent of data influence on model significance, a new approach is presented that simulates adversarial training using minimal modifications to actual data. This enables a deeper analysis of how feature importance can be manipulated. A combination of User Relevance and Adversarial Influence serves as a basis for assessing the validity of significance rankings. Through experiments involving multiple classification models and datasets, including extensive user studies, the proposed framework effectively validates the ability of features with the highest significance to distinguish good behavior from bad behavior.

Minimally invasive surgery has been greatly enhanced by the application of computer-assisted technologies, which have been particularly effective in identifying and outlining surgical tools. Although traditional methods such as contouring and contour detection have been widely utilized, they often struggle with delivering precise and consistent results in real-time during the procedure. This research explores various machine learning and deep learning techniques to enhance 2D surgical tool identification and detection in real-time during laparoscopic surgery. Multiple algorithms were evaluated to determine their performance, which was tested through a comprehensive dataset comprising 119 surgical procedures across seven different specialties. This dataset was uniquely designed to ensure diverse lighting, camera settings, and tool types, which were then used to simulate real-world operating room conditions. The results indicated that the CascadeRNN architecture achieved the highest mean average precision of 97.4% for tool identification and 84.4% for detection, which was followed by other methods such as a custom-made model and pre-trained networks such as ResNet and MobileNet. These techniques were then used for detection after simulating real-world operating room conditions, which yielded varying levels of performance, which were then ranked from highest to lowest as Custom-made model, CascadeRNN, ResNet, MobileNet, and SiamMask.

One of the most significant tasks in video understanding is recognizing individuals. A commonly used evaluation benchmark for this purpose is the Person Re-Identification (Re-ID) dataset, which however suffers from limited scale. To address this, a large-scale unsupervised video Re-ID dataset construction and assessment methodology are developed, focusing on extensive experiments with diverse data variations. A primary objective is to pursue large-scale unsupervised Re-ID dataset construction, accomplished by adapting Contrastive Learning to the Re-ID task. Initially, image pairs are pre-selected and filtered using CLIP features before fine-tuning with contrastive loss. Notably, this approach yields substantial performance gains. A key finding is that increasing the dataset size results in notable improvements in F-score by up to 43% when moving from 100 to 1000 individuals. Furthermore, model training on the proposed video corpus leads to 12-fold improvement in F-score compared to the best published methods on the MRB benchmark.

This study presents a new Bayesian probability model called the Realized Threshold Assessment GARCH (RTAGARCH) framework, which is a framework for forecasting extreme market events. RTAGARCH builds on the traditional Threshold GARCH (TGARCH) framework and uses a different approach to model market volatility. Unlike TGARCH, which presumes that model parameters are evenly distributed, RTAGARCH acknowledges the presence of unsampled parameters and their impact on volatility forecasts. To address this, the RTAGARCH framework employs the Dynamic Marginalization technique to eliminate unsampled parameters and generate more accurate forecasts of future volatility. The advantages of the RTAGARCH framework over the TGARCH framework are demonstrated through an analysis of the S&P 594 Value-at-Risk (VaR) forecasts, showing significant improvements in accuracy and reliability.

Evaluating the triaxiality of the Milky Way's dark matter profile is essential for a comprehensive understanding of its structure. By analyzing the pulsar timing array data, we derive the rotation curve of the Milky Way, revealing the galactic rotation constant to be $A_0 = 13.34^{+0.12}_{-0.10}\textrm{ hr}^{-1}\textrm{ rad}^{-1}$ with a $90\%$ confidence level. This precise measurement helps us understand the galaxy's overall shape and the distribution of its dark matter.

A lattice QCD simulation was conducted using two-current associations to study pseudoscalar and scalar pions. For the two-currents to annihilate into a photon in this simulation, they needed to be vector currents. The mass ratios of these particles to the nucleon were obtained and matched experimental data very closely. Furthermore, a discrepancy between the scalar and vector V-A discrepancy for the pion was revealed in this simulation.

A study analysis of available optical data for the young star XX Cha is presented, which is still on its evolutionary main sequence. In contrast to other T Tauri stars with similar properties, XX Cha exhibits a significantly broader range of accretion rates. To investigate the characteristics of XX Cha's accretion rates, a new model is developed. This model demonstrates that the observed properties of XX Cha can be attributed to its activity cycle's impact on both the observed accretion rate distribution and the luminosity of the star. Based on available data, there is a high probability that the average accretion rate of XX Cha is around $1.1 \times 10^{-8} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$, which is consistent with previous estimates. As a result, future research should take into account time-averaged quantities when investigating the connection between physical parameters of T Tauri stars and their accretion rates.

The concept of inequality of chance was first introduced by Joseph Loewenstein in 1996 and has since been variously interpreted as the inequality of resources, initial conditions, or starting lines. In this study, we integrate the inequality of chance with the inequality of effort and ability within a simple economic model that incorporates income redistribution. According to this framework, the inequality of chance encompasses both the inequality of resources and initial conditions. We found that higher levels of inequality of chance can lead to a socially optimal level of redistribution, provided that the marginal benefit of additional resources is less than or equal to $0.5$ times the marginal effect of additional effort on output. Additionally, a higher inequality of effort can lead to the inequality of chance being an optimal level of redistribution, provided that the inequality of effort is not too high. This finding may help explain the moderate levels of inequality observed in many Western democracies.

Utilizing Demazure operators, we've developed methods to derive quantum $K$-polynomials for various flag manifolds, specifically including Grassmannians and more complex spaces constructed from semisimple algebraic groups and Borel subgroups. We've also established properties of the quantum product and a more in-depth understanding of how the Bernoulli operator acts on $K$-homology. Furthermore, we've introduced combinatorial methods to address the Berman-Givental conjecture regarding the associativity of the quantum product on Grassmannians.

The vast amount of available data, despite being resourceful, can also be problematic, given that many large-scale datasets contain numerous errors, often going unnoticed until they cause issues during the training of machine learning models. However, pinpointing data issues in isolated subsets is relatively straightforward, but becomes significantly more complex when dealing with data that is part of a machine learning pipeline. In this research, we aim to identify data problems by examining the data's overall contribution to the final output of a machine learning pipeline. We propose a novel approach, known as DataDebug, which leverages the concept of Shapley values to analyze how individual data items contribute to the overall performance of the pipeline. We demonstrate that DataDebug can effectively pinpoint issues in data, even when it is part of a complex pipeline involving data transformations and model selection. Furthermore, we show that DataDebug outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

This study explores the connection between radio sources and the dynamics of their parent stellar systems in four Galactic globular clusters, focusing on Trappist 1, M4, and M5. Utilizing data from the MAVERIC survey, researchers conducted a in-depth examination of the velocity distributions of X-ray binaries, millisecond pulsars, and the overall cluster population. They discovered an anomalous presence of X-ray binaries with velocities up to 100 km/s in M4 and M5, contrasting with the high density of sources within their Roche lobes in Trappist 1. This discrepancy is attributed to energy equipartition among neutrinos and photons, as well as mass segregation driven by spiral arms, Dynamos, and precession, indicating a significant role for dynamic processes in determining the origin of radio sources in galactic globular clusters.

We propose a novel representation called Multi-Element Graphs to effectively
capture higher-order relationships in learning tasks. Our approach builds upon
this representation by proposing the Guided Hypergraph Reconstruction
algorithm to convert complex connections into manageable ones for a traditional
learning framework. The proposal involves a dual strategy of a static GHR and a
dynamic GHR, which can be used to solve a variety of problems such as classification,
multi-class segmentation and image generation, through either fully connected
or sparsely connected graphs. The proposed method demonstrates improved
performance compared to state-of-the-art techniques on multiple datasets across
different applications.

We propose an entropy-based method for measuring directional light emissions in microcavity lasers. This approach quantifies the entropy of photons within a specific spatial area, enabling a binary classification of the emission pattern. By comparing the entropy values to that of uniform distribution, we can determine the directionality of the light. This simple and intuitive metric is easy to calculate and provides a clear threshold for directionality. We demonstrate our method's efficacy through Monte Carlo simulations and experimental data, showing a strong correlation between our entropy values and commonly used directionality definitions. Our proposed directionality factor can be determined using only the entropy values, offering an alternative to more complex methods. Furthermore, our framework can be extended to other systems, making it a versatile tool for assessing directionality in various contexts.

We examine thermal atomic transitions that are illuminated by intense light and exhibit collective interactions by applying a semi-classical model in the strong light regime.  When the light intensity is high enough, a more precise understanding is required as the atomic ensemble enters a regime where non-linear effects come into play.  Although the standard semi-classical model provides useful insights into moderate intensity regimes, it ultimately fails as it erroneously allows the atomic polarization to increase indefinitely with rising light intensity.  By analyzing two atomic systems with varying interatomic distances, we both experimentally and theoretically investigate mid to high intensity regimes.  By measuring light scattering at a range of light intensities, we observe the transition from a regime dominated by atomic interactions to one governed by light saturation effects.  This regime can be successfully modeled using a modified semi-classical model taking into account non-linear effects.  However, at higher intensity regimes, the theoretical predictions of even this modified model diverge from experimental observations, indicating the need for a quantum treatment of the highly excited atomic ensemble under intense light.

Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning poses significant challenges due to an unknown number of agents and diverse actions, which can lead to large action spaces and a variety of underlying dynamics. In this context, offline learning is particularly beneficial as it eliminates the need for simultaneous exploration. A new class of offline multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithms has been introduced, specifically designed for environments with uncoordinated actions and varying dynamics. These algorithms leverage the concepts of good paths and action-based value functions to efficiently capture the essence of the learning process, thus reducing the effective action space. A specific algorithm within this class proposes using context clusters to support transferability among similar sub-problems. The theoretical analysis of this class of algorithms results in an epsilon approximation optimality, demonstrating their potential and efficiency. Furthermore, additional information and removal of assumptions can significantly improve their performance. The practical application of these algorithms is also demonstrated through comprehensive offline training and application of the resulting model.

We introduce a novel alignment method for MV images, specifically planning MV images in 2D or 3D space. Due to advancements in imaging technology and treatment techniques, using 2D/3D image guidance therapy improves treatment outcomes. Aligning megavoltage images is crucial for optimizing treatment results. Our approach involves using Convolutional Neural Networks to shift images, which can be done manually but often feels intuitive. We used two CNN models to implement this, namely Deconvolutional Deformable Convolutional Network and Convolutional Neural Network Regressor, which achieve high accuracy in both manual and automatic alignment, as shown in our study using nine head images, where the models' accuracy reached 97.1% and 94.1% respectively.

We investigate the nonlocal characteristics of single-particle steering, a phenomenon arising from measurements of spatially separated particles that carry the same state. Our analysis reveals that single-particle steering can exhibit genuinely nonlocal behavior, undermining local realism. Surprisingly, we find that even when the particle performs observations in an intermediate position between the two measurement locations, the nonlocal effects of single-particle steering remain genuinely intact.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence and two technologies into the Internet of Vehicles is essential for enhanced driving experiences, however, multiple security threats jeopardize data privacy and system integrity. A Federated Learning framework can address these concerns, by preventing single-server control and allowing for private model training. Despite the potential of this framework, various components such as Blockchain, Privacy-Preserving techniques, and Artificial Intelligence remain untested for their effectiveness in a unified system. Conducting an examination of research studies on Blockchain-enabled Federated Learning systems for the Internet of Vehicles revealed several proposed designs, Blockchain implementations, security measures, and performance assessments. Identifying key security concerns and performance evaluations revealed areas for improvement in these systems, and highlighted the need for more research into real-world testing and cost-efficiency assessments.

V392 Persei, an extremely luminous nova discovered back in 2018, is an unusual object that scientists are eager to study. V392 Persei exhibits a \gamma-ray burst in 2018, positioning it among a rare group of \gamma-ray-emitting novae. Since its discovery, V392 Persei has been observed using optical, X-ray, and \gamma-ray telescopes. V392 Persei is not an typical LNova due to its high velocity and abundance of heavy elements. V392 Persei also does not fit the profile of a BrSource due to its lack of an accretion disk and its high rate of X-ray and \gamma-ray radiation. By analyzing the spectral characteristics of V392 Persei, a model was developed in which a rapidly spinning neutron star emits X-rays that are then focused by a novae shock onto the poles of the stellar surface, creating \gamma-rays. V392 Persei is an unusual hybrid object that exhibits characteristics of both BrSources and LNovae, and it is one of the first known cases of a \gamma-ray-emitting dwarf nova eruption. V392 Persei is a unique source that could provide insight into the physical processes at play during both nova and dwarf nova eruptions.

In quantum computing, incorporating more than two qubits into a single operation becomes increasingly difficult as the number of qubits grows, largely due to the difficulty of synchronizing the timing of multiple quantum devices. Researchers are investigating whether using two-qubit operations on encoded qubits within an error correction code, such as the toric code, could compensate for this limitation by offering a computational power equivalent to multi-qubit gates. In this study, we identify and analyze a family of convex shapes called caltrops that, when used as boundaries for quantum operations, are equivalent in descriptive capability to multi-qubit gates in the toric code. Furthermore, we provide a conversion method to translate these fused two-qubit interactions into multi-qubit gates in the code space, and confirm the superiority of both classes of operations over just two-qubit gates on unencoded qubits through a specific demonstration of the quantum MIP* = MIP* theorem.

This research proposes a codebook creation and feedback encoding method for the uplink transmission of cellular communication, specifically targeting the efficiency of processing in time-division duplexing. To address the high computational cost of joint optimization, a two-step strategy is implemented, starting with generating a set of codewords that maximizes average sum-rate through clustering on a subset of channel realizations. subsequently, a selective feedback mechanism encodes information by transmitting the strongest codebook index and associated precoder information, which is optimized for a particular channel state. Finally, the proposed method's performance is validated to exceed current industry standards, demonstrating enhanced spectral efficiency and reduced average processing time when compared to existing commercial techniques.

In a two-dimensional disordered metal, a weak magnetic field can cause a nonequilibrium current to flow around its perimeter when subjected to light, and this effect, known as the Hall conductance, is particularly robust in certain insulators, such as the 3D Hofstadter model, where it can reach quantized values. To better understand this, we performed calculations using a lattice model and found that this current persists even when we take into account the finite lifespan of electronic excitations, and this effect is linked to a balanced, spontaneously generated current that exists on the surface of this system.

Our findings suggest that this robust Hall conductance arises from a localized, balanced current that flows on the surface of the system, and this phenomenon occurs in multiple states, including those with strong external currents imposed, and this effect is new and represents a type of chirally polarized dipole moment that has not been observed before, which could have significant implications for the development of topological superconductors on the surface of this system.

The Bondi mass loss formula is widely accepted and correct for a specific type of star, but its applicability to another category of stars is not as clear. A key aspect of the equation is a coefficient that is determined by the specific characteristics of the star, which can vary greatly, from nearly zero to more than ten times the value predicted by the equation. This study aims to establish the minimum value of this coefficient based on the fundamental laws of physics, which can be separately examined for each of its components, including the star's rotation, size, and shape, as well as the type of radiation it emits. For several types of stars, this study calculates the mass loss due to radiation, taking into account the effects of rotation and reprocessing of radiation, and determines the corresponding bondi coefficient, based on the star's spin and thrust, which can range from nearly zero to more than ten times the value predicted by the equation for these stars.

We investigate the impact of nuclear star clusters (NSCs) on the structure and evolution of massive, gas-rich star clusters at the heart of early galaxies. Our findings reveal that hosting galaxies with central supermassive black holes and located at the universe's high redshift can significantly alter these clusters' evolution. A high density of stars within a galaxy nucleus forces stars into close encounters and can cause them to fall towards a supermassive black hole where they are destroyed by tidal forces. As a result, clusters within galaxy nuclei experience extended lifespans, retain more massive stars for longer periods, and are more likely to produce Tidal Disruption Events. However, we find that clusters without NSCs undergo rapid dynamical collapse, resulting in gravitational wave production from merging black holes and stacking of stellar mass at the center of the galaxy. This process also leads to clumps of stars that merge with each other and the supermassive black hole, all generating gravitational waves that can be detected by third-generation detectors like Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer.

The satellite detector known as GECAM is specialized in detecting gravitational waves and is designed to detect bursts of gamma-rays, potentially from supernovae that produce a bright burst of radiation. GECAM's ability to detect such radiation is dependent on a precise system called the LeCrate, which is responsible for triggering the detector and is calibrated using a pre-programmed surge table. To test the accuracy of this system, a portable simulator was built to mimic the effects of a gamma-ray burst on the satellite detector. By using a large array of detectors, this simulator can accurately reproduce the exact conditions of a gamma-ray burst, allowing researchers to test GECAM's performance and ensure its accuracy.

This paper investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA and its generalized form, $\text{BMOA}_{p}$, with focus on BMOA_{1}, examining their generator and associated integral operators with a specific symbol, and determining when semigroups of T_y remain within BMOA and BMOA_{p}, while exploring connections to the growth of $\phi$.

Despite the vast volume of published research, there's uncertainty about its qualitative impact on human knowledge. A common metric for scholarly contribution is citation count, especially when aggregated to form indices of research productivity. Since the 1980s, to achieve high-citation rates, new areas of science without established benchmarks have emerged, such as machine learning in the 2020s. In contrast, fields like physics and chemistry, known for their substantial knowledge bases, do not typically produce highly cited research. This observation suggests a disparity between scholarly productivity and knowledge amount.

In this study, we examine a wireless transmission system that utilizes an relay node to improve signal delivery to a legitimate receiver, while an eavesdropper intercepts the transmission between the source and the destination. By analyzing various scenarios where the eavesdropper is located, we derive closed-form expressions for the secrecy capacity and locate optimal nodes through a low computational cost method. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of adding security nodes on the system's performance and the associated costs, finding the optimal node placement to maximize the secrecy capacity. Our results are validated via simulation, providing insights into the system's behavior and the security capacity curve.

2D waveguide arrays exhibiting a non-trivial Chern number are ideal for achieving topologically protected quantum state transfer. In this research, we examine a parabolic waveguide system and discover that, unlike its classical counterpart which only displays a single isolated band, it possesses an additional isolated band in the quantum regime. In this regime, we determine that a certain integer offset in charge density is necessary to facilitate protected quantum state transfer between waveguides located at equivalent radii. Our analysis also investigates the stability of this transfer under conditions of disorder and thermal fluctuations, and discovers that saybath-induced dephasing results in protected transitions experiencing greater density excitation decay than their non-topological counterparts.

Developing a predictive control strategy for connected automated vehicles approaching a traffic signalized intersection is a complex challenge in modern transportation systems. We explored using Maximum Entropy Deep Stochastic Control to create a safety-conscious predictive controller, applying it to a realistic intersection scenario involving multiple approaches. Instead of traditional constraints, we incorporated safety as a utility function dependent on gaps between automated and human-driven vehicles. By evaluating our controller through an extensive simulation with over 1000 randomly generated scenarios, we discovered that replacing hard-constrained models with safety-oriented objectives allows for smoother interactions and more efficient use of intersection space by human drivers. As this intersection becomes more saturated with human vehicles, we found that a safety-conscious predictive controller could improve its capacity by significantly reducing the probability of rear-end collisions.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to test virtual agents, though their speed is a significant limitation. We present TextWorldExpress, a significantly enhanced version of the original TextWorld platform, with no changes to the original datasets but substantial improvements in performance. Using the original tasks, TextWorldExpress achieves a simulation speed of one million actions per second on average, approximately 10 times faster than the original platform. This substantial speed increase stems from design choices targeting minimal bottlenecks, the use of high-performance components, and the optimization of key algorithms. We publicly release TextWorldExpress as an open-source project at https://github.com/Microsoft/TextWorldExpress.

Deep learning models, particularly Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have been highly effective in processing and analyzing time-series data, including video content.  Despite their success, conventional implementation methods using matrix multiplication operations on GPU/TPU or mobile processors suffer from low computational efficiency and high energy consumption. As a result, processing large volumes of video data is energy-intensive and often leads to suboptimal system performance. To address this challenge, a novel approach is presented that integrates algorithm and hardware design to create energy-efficient LSTM implementations, capable of accurately classifying videos even with limited data. Key to this approach is the application of hierarchical Tucker listless operations on sparse hardware accelerators, allowing for more efficient factorization and storage of LSTM weights. Converting the weight matrix to a 3D tensor is found to reduce storage requirements, decrease computational operations, and enhance memory efficiency. Furthermore, a custom hardware architecture is designed to efficiently perform the proposed algorithm, resulting in significant improvements in energy consumption and overall system performance compared to conventional implementations.

In NLP tasks trained on neural networks, obtaining sufficient training data is often challenging. To overcome this challenge, researchers have proposed various data augmentation techniques that can boost dataset size by generating synthetic training samples. Though the concept of data augmentation is widely recognized成功 in computer vision, its potential in NLP has not been fully explored. This research focuses on evaluating different NLP strategies in a comprehensive and standardized setting. We assess 2 types of data augmentation techniques across 3 categories of tasks. Our experiments reveal that certain simple techniques can enhance model performance when training datasets are limited, while our publicly available resources can facilitate future studies on data augmentation in NLP.

We demonstrate the validity of a novel hypothesis, the feeble gravity conjecture, which posits that in a consistent conformal field theory, the operator charge must be bounded above by a specific value proportional to the central charge, and we verify this proportionality is less than 8/3. This proposed bound directly correlates with the feeble gravity conjecture in string theory, suggesting the charge-to-tension ratio of a charged object must be less than a specific value, and we investigate the underlying reasons why the operator charge is subject to the proportionality defined by the central charge. To support this, we introduce the concept of convexity of charged operators, arguing that in conformal field theories, the expected behavior of charged operators is governed by the highest possible tension state, and then provide the exact proportionality for the charged operator norm in unitary 2D CFTs, pre-unitary 2D CFTs, and heavy-light bootstrap setups. This research contributes to advancing the convexity-based method, and we discuss its relation to the F-G inequality and outline further directions for exploration.

We present a novel strategy for modeling multi-state quantum systems, by
equating their imaginary time evolution to that of a single-state system in a
Fermi-liquid state under 'quantum fictitious time' evolution. This method enables
the application of established single-state quantum simulation techniques to
multi-state quantum systems, overcoming their inherent difficulties such as
large ground-state wave function cancellations and exponential growth of
computational requirements. We demonstrate the theoretical underpinnings of this
approach and derive a critical threshold for system size where the behavior of the
single-state Fermi-liquid system accurately reflects the multi-state case. We
also propose using a 'quantum fictitious time' gradient to bridge the two scenarios
and investigate the resulting effects, particularly regarding particle-number
superfluid components. Finally, we compare first-principles and multi-state
simulation results for a two-band Hubbard model, showcasing the potential
applications and limitations of our proposed strategy.

Given a local ring $(R, \mathfrak m)$ of positive characteristic, we establish a method to determine the precise value of its tight Hilbert polynomial $H_R(\lambda)$ for sufficiently large $\lambda$. This finding is relevant as it brings us closer to resolving an open question first raised by Cox in 2009 about whether there exists a way to calculate the precise value of $H_R(\lambda)$ for all $\lambda \geq 0$. Additionally, we identify characteristics of F-pure and F-rational local rings using the function $\epsilon R(\lambda)$. These features allow us to identify an F-rational local domain as one with a sufficiently large twist of its canonical module being $+\infty$, and a local ring regular in singularity type as one with a sufficiently large tight Hilbert polynomial equal to that of a unique polynomial.

The increasing importance of electricity market auxiliary services is driving the need for demand response participation. However, current market mechanisms often fail to consider demand response's potential contribution to these services. This paper presents a new model that accounts for demand response's involvement in providing auxiliary services and develops a supply chain game theoric framework to model market interactions. This framework can inform policy design by highlighting a government's ability to influence supply. A case study is used to calibrate the model and demonstrate its effectiveness, while also providing supply, demand, and utility data. The results show that the government can influence demand response consumption by providing auxiliary services, a finding that may help promote more efficient use of resources and promote the development of more sustainable energy systems.

Let K be a field of positive characteristic, and let R be an algebraic extension of K times the rational numbers. In the ring R, we determine the conditions under which a polynomial of the form x^n + (sum of coefficients times powers of another polynomial g(x))) has the property that it evaluates to an irreducible polynomial when any two non-constant polynomials f and g from R are substituted. Additionally, we find a condition for when the m-th iterated composition of two polynomials f and g evaluates to a polynomial that is irreducible.

This paper explores the nonperturbative aspects of QCD for calculating standard model Higgs boson pair production through the bbWW* final state, utilized as a primary search pathway for beyond standard model Higgs at the LHC. By applying the matrix element method, we offer an accurate and computationally efficient computation of differential cross sections, yielding results that accurately match full next-to-next-to-leading order calculations for various invariant mass distributions. By utilizing this approach, we can precisely determine Higgs boson pair and standard model Higgs plus two Higgs bosons differential distributions, allowing us to derive robust predictions for Higgs boson pair signal yields, taking into account all relevant phase space correlations.

We evaluate the impact of new scalar particles in type-II Two-Higgs-Doublet Models on the precision $e^+e^-\to Zh$ and associated suppression of the Higgs boson's decay to $\gamma\gamma$. To accurately predict these processes, a fully modular interface has been developed within the HHiggs package, interfacing with the CPPFit fitting group to obtain revised Standard Model values for the Higgs branching ratios. Our analysis utilizes updated predictions for electron-positron collisions at center-of-mass energies of 240, 250, and 350 GeV. We examine the constraints that precision investigations can place on the vacuum expectation values and the coupling matrix between the Higgs doublets in the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model. In particular, we demonstrate the capacity for current and upcoming electron-positron experiments to constrain this new scalar sector, provided its mass spectrum falls within a specific mid-range.

Saturn's upper atmosphere is divided into six alternating bands aligned with its planet's rotation, forming six long-lasting polar vortices at the end of Saturn's 10.7-Earth-day seasons.  During the 7.4-Earth-day winters, massive polar vortices gather at the poles, creating the largest structures in Saturn's summer atmosphere.  In this study, we use observations from the Saturn-based spacecraft Cassini to track the northern polar atmosphere of Jupiter as it transitions from its 2018 summer to its 2019 winter.  Our analysis shows that the warm polar atmosphere begins to cool in the stratosphere above the equator, forming a vortex that gradually descends into the colder lower atmosphere, where it remains for the duration of the season.  As the planet rotates, this large polar feature encloses six small hexagons, creating a striking pattern in Saturn's northern atmosphere.  Our findings provide the first evidence of a polar hexagon in Saturn's atmosphere and a detailed look at how the polar atmosphere changes from summer to winter.

For a specific set of parameters, researchers have previously obtained exact solutions for the time-dependent nonlinear Schrödinger equation outside a bounded domain in R^d, where 2 ≤ d is an even number smaller than 4, and the solution should satisfy a given boundary condition on a fixed set and an exponential time-growth condition. A key property of this problem is its ability to demonstrate non-uniformity in local behavior for a variety of initial conditions, specifically in its ability to provide a counterexample to a well-known result in the theory of the time-dependent nonlinear Schrödinger equation, which asserts that solutions with sub-cubic nonlinearity cannot exhibit explosive behavior in a finite time.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero reductions of a smooth affine variety, which is defined by exponential-genus complexity and possesses positive-dimensional characteristic-zero parameter space, admits a semi-parametric characteristic-zero reduction that matches its characteristic-positive target up to a uniform polynomial bound. This result is particularly useful in establishing positive-characteristic isomorphism invariants for characteristic-zero affine varieties.

The metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ exhibits notable differences when occurring in bulk form or within confined layers, and now also shows distinct differences when happening in any intermediate scenario, and the reason behind this is not yet fully understood, and and the study focuses on V$_2$O$_3$(0001) films grown on the SrTiO$_3$(001) surface and contains X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and low-energy electron diffraction findings, and and indicates a significant difference in V$_2$O$_3$'s electronic and atomic outer layer structure compared to its bulk counterpart, and and indicates that modifications to the V$_2$O$_3$'s outer layer can be attributed to interactions with the substrate and an oxygen layer, and and suggests that V$_2$O$_3$'s outer layer is unstable and and can be controlled, and and suggests an investigation of V$_2$O$_3$'s intermediate state, and and contains theoretical calculations that indicate an oxygen layer is present due to vacuum conditions, and and suggests that more research is required to fully understand the V$_2$O$_3$'s intermediate state, and and contains DFT calculations that indicate an oxygen layer is present, and and suggests that this is due to the impact of V$_2$O$_3$'s surface, and and suggests that this can be attributed to substrate V $d$-orb

We employ both numerical and analytical techniques to investigate a non-integrable two-component Gross-Pitaevskii equation in one dimension, representing two distinct quantum states of matter held together by an optical barrier. In this study, we find an approximate decay law for quantum systems with varying particle numbers, indicating a rapid approach to their predictable dual-soliton behavior. We also develop a simplified, non-linear method to predict the two-peaked structure of Bose-Einstein condensation, by analyzing the system's interaction and density.

We create a linearization functor for full linearization that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines necessary and sufficient conditions for a k-fold vector bundle to be the full linearization of a specific type of graded bundle. We establish relationships between these conditions and their implications, showing how they connect to the structure of graded bundles.

Let G be the group G(Ares) = U(2, R) or U(3, R). We examine the general linear group's non-zero, semi-simple elements in a specific region of A, denoted as P G(Delta). These elements can be decomposed into disjoint orbits under the action of U(Delta), with each orbit corresponding to a distinct, diagonal element in a different subspace of D. The set D can be divided into regions, denoted as D', where the measure dD can be adjusted to a measure, denoted as dD', by a function, denoted as c, which satisfies the equation c(D') = integral over D' of the orbital integrals of generic elements of G. The measure c can be used to adjust the I(Delta)-invariance of the measure dD'. The result is an extension of a prior proof by G. Harder. The original proof was for the group U(1, R), and the proof in the paper is for the groups U(2, R) or U(3, R), and the proof is with a compactness argument, and the proof is with a local extension of the Geometric Multiplicity Conjecture, and the proof is with a detailed, and the proof is with a detailed, and the proof is with a detailed, and the proof is with a detailed, and the proof is with a detailed, and the proof is with a detailed, and

Nuclear reactions produce a brief, hot, and expanding region called a nuclear fireball, which is thought to be where essential data for creating accurate atomic nuclei models can be found. A key feature of this fireball is its selforganization, a process in which the nuclei atoms arrange themselves into a structured pattern known as a crystal. Although the existence of a crystal has long been predicted, evidence of this phenomenon remains elusive. We present a novel technique to detect the integrity of this crystal by using x-ray scattering and scattering in simulation reactions. Through this method, we were able to accurately reproduce the complex relationship between intensity and energy in simulated reactions, providing a direct evidence of the crystal's existence and its persistence even after the reactions have occurred. This discovery has far-reaching implications, as it paves the way for a more in-depth understanding of the nuclear fireball.

This research develops a theoretical framework to analyze the performance limitations of quantum error correction circuits, specifically focusing on how faults occur and influence the system. By creating an analytical model that accounts for different types of errors, including those that happen during the operation of quantum logical gates, the study establishes an upper limit on the error rates necessary for a functional code. Furthermore, the concept of quantum threshold is directly related to the critical parameters found in analogous classical statistical systems. Moreover, this relationship provides valuable insights into designing optimized codes and can guide the development of more efficient quantum error correction circuits, as demonstrated with the surface code.

Recent theoretical predictions suggest that elemental tellurium could form two distinct atom-thick versions known as monolayers and double monolayers, or tellurene. We have used first-principles calculations to investigate the structural, electronic, and topological properties of various configurations of clean and chemically modified tellurene, including substitutions with lithium, sodium, beryllium, magnesium and oxygen. Our findings indicate that strained monolayer and certain functionalized configurations like Na-t and O-t are likely to be large-gap 2D topological insulators. The topological gap in the Gr-t configuration of monolayer tellurene is notably large at 1.14 eV, making it an ideal platform for experimentally observing the rich quantum phenomena associated with this material.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element method to model single-phase Darcy flow in a fractured porous media with transversal fractures. Our method combines a standard discrete domain with a level set discretization, accurately capturing the geometry of the fractures. As a result, the discrete problem's complexity grows linearly with the number of fractures. We provide a rigorous error analysis for the method and demonstrate its effectiveness through several examples in two dimensions.

A novel device known as the spin switch has been proposed, which relies on a unique spiral magnetic layer with magnetization arranged in a C-shaped pattern. The device is built on a sandwich structure incorporating a spiral layer and occurs when the spin-polarized current's orientation is rotated by the spiral layer. The rotation can be achieved through the use of an adjacent spiral coil carrying a spin-polarized current. Notably, the spin switch requires only a single magnetic layer and is robust against thermal fluctuations, making it suitable for integration with a spiral memory layer in a racetrack layout.

A Bayes factor stands as a unique method in statistics, partly due to its ability to accommodate any prior information, which also presents a significant challenge. This characteristic ambiguity can be addressed by developing the concept of a Bayes factor workflow, encompassing various strategies such as adapting Bayes factors to specific contexts, combining multiple expert opinions, utilizing Bayes factor ranges, and applying model selection techniques. A proposed framework for exchanging Bayes factor-based evidence effectively utilizes a score-based system, which can be applied to models and enables the integration of model probabilities through established criteria like the Bayes optimal method. This integration process is facilitated by a set of established rules for comparing, ranking, and making coherent inferences about models with Bayes factors.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "hence" are frequently
employed to convey connections between sentences, whether that be a
consequence, a shift, a conclusion, or another argument. This research
examines whether these discourse indicators can be utilized to enhance
modern systems' ability to generate texts that convey arguments effectively.
We tested whether incorporating a discourse indicator during generation,
tailored to the specific relation between texts, would improve the discourse
marker's ability to convey the intended semantic relationship compared to
leaving it unspecified. We also investigated the effect of the frequency of
a particular discourse indicator on its ability to convey a specific meaning.
We compiled a novel dataset consisting of pairs of texts from a well-known
dataset, annotated with a discursive marker where one was available, along
with the relationship it established, allowing for exploration of the
effect of incorporating the discourse indicator and whether models would
learn to favor lower-frequency markers. We developed a comprehensive set of
evaluations to assess the relationship between texts produced with the
discourse indicator's relation explicitly modeled, generated with the
appropriate discourse indicator, left without one, or no indicator's
semantic relationship considered. These evaluations were conducted using
three established discursive tools as well as a comprehensive large-scale
evaluation. We found that models with the help of the SENSEVAL suite of
evaluations could accurately predict the use of a discursive indicator in
about 60% of

We investigated the spectroscopic properties of a diamond crystal containing a nitrogen vacancy (NV) center, raising the diamond's temperature to 500°C in a stepwise process.  By measuring the zero-phonon line shift and photoluminescence intensity at various temperatures, our data revealed a significant decline in both factors as the temperature increased, with a particularly sharp drop in photoluminescence intensity between 250°C and 350°C.  Our research implies that an elevated temperature of around 250-300°C may be more optimal for certain applications involving NV centers, as it could reduce the need for additional broadening factors in determining temperature by as much as 40%.

A key aspect of the brain's processing system is its ability to learn through local signals. One of the most extensively researched models of learning is Hebbian learning, in which the connections between neurons are modified based on the coincidence of pre- and post-synaptic activity. Despite its simplicity, Hebbian learning can lead to instability and an uncontrolled increase in firing rates. This issue can be mitigated by incorporating a lateral inhibitory mechanism, such as competition between neurons for limited resources. This concept is known as "winner-take-all" dynamics. Our study aims to examine whether a specific type of neuron called the pyramidal cell can utilize a form of Hebbian learning to selectively strengthen its input connections with other neurons that contribute to its victory in competitive situations. Using a mathematical framework, AIscociated Learning was modeled, and it was discovered that this type of learning can be stable, produce uncontrollable increase in firing rates, and allow for a winner-based competitive dynamics, thus making it a promising candidate for explaining how neurons learn from local signals.

A detailed investigation of a spin model on the triangular lattice was performed,
where the S=3/2 Heisenberg interaction was studied through a sigma-model formulation.
The formulation was evaluated numerically using the lattice Monte Carlo approach,
which yielded results that closely matched analytical and numerical findings from other methods.
Key advantages of this method include the ability to easily account for an SU(3) symmetry-breaking field,
obtain the spin system's entropy, and potential extensions to spin systems on bipartite lattices.
These could enable simultaneous examination of both NEEL and CO order types,
with the potential to unravel the mechanism behind the spiral phase observed in Li$_2$RuO$_3$.

A novel implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently compute ground-state wave functions and total energies for systems governed by arbitrary central potentials. By representing single-particle states as linear combinations of B-spline basis functions, the HF equations are solved for the optimal coefficients and optimal potential in an iterative process. Key features of this implementation include a large, pre-generated B-spline basis from the DSplineLib library, available in both serial and parallel formats. Extensive comparisons with established results from atoms to applications electron gas demonstrate the method's accuracy, matching or exceeding the accuracy of previous HF methods while significantly reducing computational time.

We have developed a universal standard to identify the potential for explosive synchronization in diverse populations of oscillators, which operates independently of specific model details or dimensionality. This criterion signals the impending collapse of a stable system when met, characterized by a notable acceleration in synchronization progression near the threshold. Our analysis demonstrates that this phenomenon is caused by a marked acceleration in the growth of a specific network, occurring when the interplay between feedback connections and natural frequency variations results in the system's collapse into a highly interconnected state.

Nonnegative factorization is a popular matrix decomposition technique that has various applications, yet it generally presents a non-convex optimization challenge.  We investigate the geodesic curvature of the stochastic manifold used in matrix factorization and factor analysis to better understand the landscape of objective functions and their critical points.  We demonstrate that introducing a regularization term based on the log-determinant of $A^TA$ can transform saddle points into local minima and trap points into geodesically convex basins of attraction.  As a result, finding high-quality solutions through local optimization methods becomes feasible and efficient, as illustrated by our theoretical analysis and numerical experiments for both $a$-Factor Analysis and $a$-Low Rank Regression.

A graph is considered robustly edge-colorable with k colors if it possesses an edge-coloring that can be restored with fewer than k colors after removing a single edge. In the realm of k-critical bipartite graphs of degree 3, a graph is viewed as an indicator of imperfect edge-recoloring when it exhibits symmetry between its two subsets of vertices. The primary purpose of this study is to introduce a bipartite graph with three edges and each vertex connected to three other vertices, thus providing a counterexample to a conjecture by Costello and Wormald, suggesting that highly symmetric k-critical bipartite graphs of degree 3 might be exceptionally rare or non-existent.

Let $q$ be an integer greater than one, and let $\chi$ denote a reduced Dirichlet character with a modulus of $q$. The $L$-function $L(s,\chi)$ is defined by the series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{\chi(n)}{n^s}$ for any complex number $s$. This study focuses on novel identities associated with $L(2,\chi)$, which can be expressed as $-\frac{\pi^2}{6q^2}\sum_{m=1}^{q-1}\sum_{k=1}^{q}\frac{\{\frac{km}{q}\}\{\frac{km-1/2}{q}\}}{\sin\frac{\pi k}{q}\sin\frac{\pi m}{q}}\chi(k)\overline{\chi}(m)$, where the notation $\{\cdot\}$ signifies the fractional part of a given number. When the Dirichlet character $\chi$ is reduced to the modulus one, this formula is reinterpreted to prove an alternative proof for an inequality established by Crandall.

Detailed analysis of signal characteristics allows for particle mass determination.  As a result, particles produced by GRS can still be accurately categorized as either secure or unsecure depending on whether their production rate exceeds particle decay.  Assuming the particle's lifetime exceeds its distance to decay, an unsecure particle's abundance grows in line with the GRS length.  We explore the impact of gravitational wave emission on particles linked to gravitational anomalies.  Reducing this impact by an order of magnitude allows for particle equilibrium with the Big Bang background, despite having similar production and decay rates.  We also discuss constraints on dark matter, the equivalence principle, and proton decay, along with strategies to detect these particles.

The movement of microswimmers in the presence of asymmetrical bodies and varying properties for their swimming tails influences how they move through fluids, a key area of study in the field of active matter.  Researchers are paying close attention to swimming in non-newtonian fluids, paying special attention to the effects of viscoelasticity on the movement of swimmers with asymmetrical bodies.  Researchers have found that viscoelasticity causes thigmotaxis - where viscoelasticity pushes swimming cells towards container walls.  However, the relationship between viscoelasticity and a swimming creature's directional movement has been found to depend on the nature of the viscoelasticity and the symmetry of the swimming creature.  With a deeper understanding of viscoelasticity's effects on swimming, there may be a potential for viscoelasticity to be used to guide and control the viscoelasticity's impact on swimming.  A significant difference was found in the elasticity's impact on the viscoelastic torque that influences viscoelastic tumbling.  Varying the degree of asymmetry in a swimming creature's shape, we also observed that the elasticity's impact on the viscoelastic torque that influences viscoelastic tumbling is also affected.  Using a microswimmer that has a viscoelastic torque, we found the viscoelastic tumbling is completely suppressed at a specific asymmetry. We investigated whether genetic algorithms can accurately predict Nash equilibrium in a well-established Cournot game on a one-dimensional line, where a population of players chooses both a production level and a location. We employed a cocooned genetic algorithm to replicate the evolution process and found that it could predict the Nash equilibrium of this one-dimensional Cournot game with a margin of error under ten percent. Furthermore, we demonstrated that our algorithm is robust to changes in the number of generations and population sizes.

The growing volume of text information is causing knowledge representation structures to fall short, necessitating a transition to extraction methods capable of transforming raw data into structured knowledge. Ontology learning has long been the preferred mechanism for this transformation, but existing approaches are limited to processing individual entities or relations, disregarding the interconnections that exist between all elements. This study introduces a novel method, called Deep Learner, which is based on a Long Short-Term Memory network and enables the identification of multiple entities and relations from text passages. The proposed method is now the standard by which future text-data extraction methods will be measured, and has been recognized as such by the Community Tool Wiki.

A new concept, Nonequilibrium Statistical Mechanics, is introduced to study systems far from equilibrium. On two complete graphs, we introduce an Ising-doped elector model and find a phase transition at a point on the equator of the H-S sphere. This transition, occurring without an external magnetic field, is located at the North pole of the H-S sphere. It indicates that the system reaches a critical, highly entangled state at this specific condition. This finding reveals that NSEM can capture the dynamics of systems near equilibrium.

A mathematical model is created to study how airborne pathogens spread through a population affected by environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, and wind speed. This model builds upon previous research and incorporates changes in virus survival due to different weather conditions and aerial virus movement caused by wind. It is observed that cold temperatures and high humidity can slow down the spread of viruses despite increased time people spend outdoors in winter, as seen with influenza. In contrast, warm winters in higher altitudes lead to more severe respiratory infections despite lower outdoor activity. Our model predicts similar patterns and confirms these results with existing data. Furthermore, the model shows how these dynamics can be influenced by other factors such as human behavior and the rate of aerosule evaporation, which can be affected by temperature and humidity.

Causal relationships between inputs and outputs can lead to more reliable predictions, particularly in critical applications such as medical and transportation systems, where accurately capturing uncertainty is vital. This necessitates developing methods to measure the reliability of predictions made by machine learning models. This paper presents an initial framework for exploring ways to measure prediction uncertainty in machines learning models trained through data, based on recent advancements in Cram\'er-Rao bound and Bayesian prediction. It examines the effectiveness of popular uncertainty measurement methods in relation to these theories. Furthermore, it proposes three novel approaches that integrate the principles of the Cram\'er-Rao bound and utilizes optimization, Monte Carlo simulations and variational inference to assess the model's performance. These proposals are evaluated using multiple benchmark datasets and a performance metric. The results highlight the proposed methods' superior performance, particularly the combination of principles from the Cram\'er-Rao bound which outperformed the leading uncertainty measurement techniques across the benchmarks. The suggested framework is made freely available and the code is publicly accessible, along with thorough details of the evaluation, to facilitate the discovery of new and effective uncertainty measurement approaches suitable for production machine learning models. The findings suggest that predicting probability distributions, as outlined in section 3.2 of the paper, is a promising strategy to explore in future research. The paper also highlights the potential of integrating the V.I. framework to explain model predictions, to be examined in upcoming studies. In a previously studied class of symbolic powers of edge ideals from oriented graphs that lack weighted edges, we extend this to incorporate weighted edges and provide a key criterion for determining when the powers $\omega(H)^s$ are equal to the ordinary powers $\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{I})_s$ of a weighted oriented hypergraph $H$. Additionally, we examine this relationship in the context of a weighted oriented tree and cycle.

Using a dual matrix, we have reformed a specific quantum matrix model potential, 
which permitted us to relate its partition function to a set of seven-plicker coordinates. 
This relationship has revealed that the matrix model correlates with a discrete form of $P^3$ space, 
and when the matrix size $N$ is considered large, the partition function can be described 
by a set of recursive equations.

Deep learning systems, specifically convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have significantly transformed fault-tolerant computing by achieving remarkable accuracy in visual task recognition, such as image classification and object detection. Despite their heightened efficiency, (re)trained CNNs are highly susceptible to hardware failures, including malfunctions and errors, which can have severe consequences, especially in critical applications like real-time vehicle navigation. This research aims to investigate the impact of CNN hardware faults on visual task accuracy and develop a statistical model to forecast accuracy degradation due to hardware faults, taking into account the networks' architectural design, dataset, data distribution, and dataset size. This forecast is based on the supervision of activation ranges, making it possible to anticipate performance loss in CNNs regardless of the specific type of hardware fault, provided the data remains unchanged. We present our findings in a comprehensive table, incorporating considerations for data in scenarios where images are subjected to external noise.

A pressing issue in the financial sector concerns companies that owe each other substantial debts with multiple creditors and debtors of their own. By leveraging netting concepts, a new approach is presented to effectually settle these financial obligations. This method was successfully applied on a large scale in the Romanian Ministry of Economy, where it determined the minimum set of transactions needed to clear mutual debts among approximately 6000 companies.

This paper addresses the Jordanian twist within the $r$-matrix framework, utilizing an Lax operator derived from the Takhajan-Felder elliptic VOA in an $r$-deformed context. By applying this operator to a direct sum of fundamental representations of $T_{{\varepsilon}|{\varepsilon}'}U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_2)$, we determine a family of commuting operators and a set of additional relations for the Jordanian-twisted $W_{1+7}_{{\varepsilon}|{\varepsilon}'}$-algebra, all of which can be uniformly expressed in terms of one parameter.

We propose a novel, language-agnostic technique for creating a common semantic space that encompasses vocabulary from numerous languages and domains. Our method, which operates on a single neural network, utilizes an unsupervised clustering algorithm to group words across different languages and domains into the same semantic space. It employs the Cluster-consistent Word Embedding (CCE) loss function, which ensures that words within each cluster have nearly identical vector representations, regardless of their language. This function builds upon the popular K-means algorithm and leverages the extensive corpora available for each individual language. As the corpora vary, additional data is not required due to the cluster-consistent nature of our approach. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed framework for both monolingual and multi-lingual settings, achieving state-of-the-art performance in multi-lingual benchmarks for zero-shot and few-shot learning.

This paper outlines the production of various particles and mesons, including pions, kaons, protons, and phi mesons, in the context of Xe-Xe collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 5.44 TeV.  A significant amount of research has been carried out to fabricate these particles and mesons. - pT spectra and dInet d$\eta$ distributions for pions, kaons, protons and phi mesons are shown for a variety of Xe-Xe collision events - Ratios of particles and mesons are also provided - Rapidity distributions for all of the above are also displayed - The production of these particles and mesons is analyzed in terms of their physical significance and potential for contributing to our understanding of the early universe.

A widely used task in building conversational assistants, Dialogue State Tracking (DST), involves reconstructing the user's goals from their dialogue history and target labels. Due to the difficulty of annotating large-scale conversational datasets, many studies rely on automatic labeling based on pre-trained language models. Unfortunately, this approach often produces inaccurate labels that reflect the most frequent label among training samples, which significantly hampers model performance. In this research, we investigate the impact of labeled data with incorrect labels on the DST task and discover that a substantial amount of label noise can lead to a decline in model performance comparable to having fewer trained samples. A neural network model with an attention mechanism is then developed to minimize the influence of label noise during training. Finally, a conversational dataset containing clear-cut examples of label noise is released to facilitate future efforts in evaluating and enhancing models designed to cope with noisy data.

Social movements are often difficult to predict and model due to their inherent complexity, particularly in situations of political instability. Following the unrest in Chile in October 2019, a non-local mathematical model was developed to examine the evolution of protesters, citizens, and dissenting individuals. This event was notable for its swift dissemination and geographical diversification. By mid-November, the movement had slowed down and become more concentrated in the south. However, the exact mechanism behind this evolution was unclear. Our model provides an explanation for this dynamic by taking into account mobility patterns, the influence of media coverage, and the conditions in neighboring regions. A stochastic simulation was also utilized to validate the predictive capabilities of the deterministic model.

This research compares the results of a straightforward analysis with two more intricate methods to evaluate the reliability of different techniques used to determine star formation rates from spectral energy distributions and confirm the effectiveness of various assumptions made during these processes.

We selected four distinct approaches to recover the fundamental properties, including the rate at which new stars are formed, from mock observatory data for one specific galaxy and found that none of these methods could accurately reproduce the true star formation rates for low-luminosity objects. In contrast, for higher-luminosity objects, only a particular combination of assumptions led to results that matched the true star formation rates.

In addition to evaluating different methods, we also compared our recovery techniques to a more common approach used in spectral energy distribution analysis and found that a direct fit to a physical model provided the most accurate representation of the data. A subsequent investigation into the impact of limited wavelength coverage on the retrieved properties revealed that including observations in the mid-infrared range was crucial for accurately determining the physical properties of galaxies.

To further illustrate our findings, we also applied these techniques to a real galaxy, UBES J1030+0715, and observed that the results it obtained using these different methods were in line with previously reported findings, including those that used a different approach to analyze the data.
